analysis.one_liner: Lets employers self-report wage violations to the Labor Department, pay back wages, and settle with workers outside of court.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; it sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee from January 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bring back the Payroll Audit Independent Determination (PAID) program, a Labor Department program first run as a pilot in 2018. An employer that found it had underpaid workers on minimum wage or overtime could self-audit, report the violation, and pay the back wages owed under a Labor Department-supervised settlement. Workers who accepted the settlement gave up their right to sue for those wages, including liquidated damages, though they could decline and keep their right to sue.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers that have underpaid workers on minimum wage or overtime. They could resolve violations by paying only the back wages owed, with no extra penalty, no liquidated damages, and no risk of a lawsuit over those violations; their self-audit materials would be shielded from court discovery, and the Labor Department could not use the application against them in an investigation. Some workers would also benefit: they would receive back wages faster than through a lawsuit, and the bill's findings argue the pilot returned more money per hour of enforcement than traditional investigations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers with wage and hour violations

how_it_helps.text: Employers could fix minimum wage and overtime violations by paying back wages through a Labor Department-supervised settlement instead of facing litigation [S2][S3].
Workers who accepted a settlement would get their unpaid wages paid in full, and the bill adds retaliation protection for workers who accept or decline a settlement offer [S3].

The bill's findings cite the 2018 pilot: 74 cases paid $4.1 million in back wages to 7,429 employees, with average back wages per case more than four times the average for traditional compliance actions [S3].
Workers could decline the settlement and preserve their private right of action in court [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who accept a settlement. Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, a worker who wins in court can recover liquidated damages equal to the back wages, effectively doubling the award. Under this program, the employer pays only the back wages, and accepting the settlement waives the worker's right to that double recovery and to sue over those violations. Workers whose employer applies and is denied would not be told by the Labor Department that they may have a claim. Employers also bear no fine or penalty beyond the wages they already owed.

drawbacks.text: Accepting a settlement waives the worker's right to liquidated damages, which under the Fair Labor Standards Act equal the back wages, so a worker could receive roughly half of what a court judgment might provide [S3].
The employer defines the scope of the violations: the Labor Department may not expand the investigation or settlement beyond what the employer identified in its own self-audit [S3].

If an application is denied, the Labor Department may not use the application information in an investigation, may not tell affected employees of their private right of action, and self-audit materials are exempt from court discovery without the employer's consent [S3].

No penalty attaches beyond paying the wages owed, which critics of self-audit programs generally argue weakens the deterrent against wage theft; the bill's own text contains no fines for the violation itself [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does deliver something real: a faster path to back pay for some workers and a compliance-help channel for employers, with a genuine choice for workers to decline and sue. But the core trade favors employers. The program strips out liquidated damages and penalties, lets the employer define the scope of its own violations, and keeps the self-audit hidden from courts and, in denied cases, from the workers themselves. On balance it reads as a liability-reduction mechanism for employers with a worker-payback attached, rather than the reverse.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never held a markup or brought it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Elise Stefanik introduced the bill on January 26, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S5].
Eleven Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The action history shows no further steps after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers with unpaid wage claims are no worse off and keep full court remedies, including liquidated damages; employers who would have used the program to settle cheaply gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, who kept full court remedies

for.name: Rep. Elise Stefanik
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reestablish the PAID program and recruited eight original Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup was held, and the bill never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support recorded; the bill stalled in a Republican-chaired committee and never came to a vote.

industries.industry: Employers with wage and hour violations (restaurants, retail, staffing, and other low-wage industries)
industries.note: The bill would let them resolve minimum wage and overtime violations by paying only the back wages owed, with no liquidated damages, penalty, or litigation risk, and shield the self-audit from discovery. The cost of wage theft to workers — who would forgo the double recovery a court can order — is the flip side of the employer's gain.

Employer settlements outside court, with claims waived on acceptance, would reduce the supply of FLSA cases that fund private enforcement of wage law. The bill's emphasis on avoiding litigation reflects that shift.
